Introductory practical on data analysis with R: the algae genotyping data

Published

December 1, 2025

Setting up key project parameters

No matter what you are doing, a quick analysis of a colleague’s data set or a complex ’omics project with multiple data type and sources. Before you even start coding, it is immensely useful to:

  • create a dedicated project folder,
  • create a RStudio project and setup version control,
  • think about the nature of the data you will handle and plan accordingly especially with regard to the ‘goals’ of the analysis,
  • organize “input data” and “results” folders separately,
  • avoid hardcoding file paths in your chunks. Use variables instead to specify paths relative to your “input data” and “results” folders.

Attach necessary packages

library("dplyr")
library("tidyr")
library("ggplot2")
library("adegenet")
library("ape")
library("vcfR")

If they are not already available on your system. Can you take care of the installation? 🤔

💭 Check the answer 🪂 
install.packages(c("adegenet", "vcfR"))

Introduction, background and questions

This notebook will record our efforts to analyse further the data generated in the “structural variation” module” with the algae dataset.

Specifically, our goals are:

  • Take a look at the quality of the output of the reads mapping stage.
  • Contrast the genotypes inferred from reads mapping and the available information on the examined algae strains.

Loading the input data in R

I/O file paths

setwd("/home/damien/Desktop/xx.CIBIG/R_training/")
dataDir <- "input" # modify to fit your own project input folder
outDir <- "output" # modify to fit your own project results folder

Download data files from a distant repository

# download from iTrop as an archive
dataArchiveUrl <- "https://itrop.ird.fr/programming_data/coding_data_CIBIG25.zip"

download.file(url = dataArchiveUrl,
              destfile = "coding_data_CIBIG25.zip")
# extract in dataDir
unzip(zipfile = "coding_data_CIBIG25.zip",
      exdir = dataDir,
      junkpaths = F)
# Take a look at the files
list.files(dataDir, recursive = TRUE)

Load algea strains metadata

In order to contrast the genotyping results with the metadata about these algea, we first need to load this info from a file that appears to be tab-separated values.

The functions above allow to inspect the content of the resulting object. It is ALWAYS good practice to spend some time making sure the input data is really what we think it is. These functions help doing that.

Clearly here, column names are intuitively easy to understand but not necessarily easy to process by code. There are too many white spaces and other special characters. We will probably need to fix that.

flagstats_files <- list.files(flagstatsDir, full.names = TRUE)

Here, we want to read a bunch of consistently formatted tabular files in a sole R object.

To do that, one would intuitively write a looping structure to iteratively load the content of individual files and dump into an object that can be grown as files are read.

While this is doable, loops are not memory efficient which can cause problems for handling large files and/or large amounts of files.

💭 Check the answer 🪂 
# loop - based solution (to be avoided in R for large amount of files)
flagstatsRaw <- NULL

for (f in flagstats_files) {
  x <- read.delim(f, header = FALSE, sep = "\t")
  x$strainId <- f
  flagstatsRaw <- rbind(flagstatsRaw, x)
}

# apply - based solution 
df_list <- lapply(flagstats_files, function(f) {
  x <- read.delim(f, header = FALSE, sep = "\t")
  x$strainId <- f
  x
})

flagstatsRaw <- do.call(rbind, df_list)

str(flagstatsRaw)

Plot reads mapping qualities across the investigated genetic diversity

Reformating raw flagstat data to prepare for plotting

Now let’s take a close look at the content of flagstatsRaw. You can use the Rstudio ‘Environment’ panel for that and also learn about a neat way to display large tables (or part of them) in a Quarto notebook.

rmarkdown::paged_table(flagstatsRaw, options = list(cols.min.print = 4))
ImportantWe use a function from the rmarkdown package that ships with RStudio.

To learn the meaning of the dataframe content and if in doubt about what to do, it may be wise to study the documentation for the command line program that generated this output: samtools flagstat. Note this specific section:

In this format the first column contains the values for QC-passed reads, the second column has the values for QC-failed reads and the third contains the category names.

OK so based on this you can rename the columns with base R syntax 🤔.

💭 Check the answer 🪂 
colnames(flagstatsRaw)
## [1] "V1"       "V2"       "V3"       "strainId"
colnames(flagstatsRaw) <- c("passed", "failed", "category", "strainId")
colnames(flagstatsRaw)
## [1] "passed"   "failed"   "category" "strainId"

Still, intuitively, passed and failed should have a numeric type, right? Is it the case? Can you guess why when readr tried to infer the type of those value columns in the first place it converted them to character? 🤔

To solve this, we need to have a sense of what values in the passed and failed columns of flagstatsRaw have characters that prevent coercion to numeric. So we will list those values using R regular expressions ("[^0-9.]" matches anything that is not a number or a dot). Because this is a bit advanced, here is the solution:

OK, so now we can diagnose the issues:

  • flagstat codes NA (Not Available) values as "N/A"
  • it looks like the values for categories expressed as a percentage contain a “%” sign.

So if we ultimately want to plot numeric values, we must get ride of those “%” characters in the corresponding value columns. For the "N/A", as.numeric() will convert them to NA anyhow (‘non-numeric strings give NA + warning’ in the example page of the help page)

How can we do that? 🤔

TipThis is a bit advanced, but we will use regular expressions to remove the “%” in the passed and failed columns and subsequently coherce them to numeric.
💭 Check the answer 🪂 
flagstatsClean$passed <- gsub(pattern = "%", replacement = "", flagstatsClean$passed)
flagstatsClean$failed <- gsub(pattern = "%", replacement = "", flagstatsClean$failed)

flagstatsClean$passed <- as.numeric(flagstatsClean$passed)
## Warning: NAs introduced by coercion
flagstatsClean$failed <- as.numeric(flagstatsClean$failed)
## Warning: NAs introduced by coercion

Now that you know how to use replacement patterns for text, take a look at the strainId column. How could you improve it ?

💭 Check the answer 🪂 
flagstatsClean$strainId <- gsub(pattern = "_flagstat.tsv", replacement = "", flagstatsClean$strainId)
flagstatsClean$strainId <- basename(flagstatsClean$strainId)
ImportantWhile you should first learn the basics of regular expressions in base R (type ?regex in the console and read the help), again, if you have to perform a lot of strings manipulations, consider the tidyverse stringr package which is really convenient.

We have made some progress but you surely have noticed the Warnings thrown by R after running your conversion commands… What is going on?

To have a sense of the read mapping quality, because the dataset is rather complex, we want to start by examining only the percentages computed by flagstat.

TipTake a close look again at the flagstat command documentation. Can this help?:

“In the tsv and json formats, these percentages are listed in separate categories mapped %, primary mapped %, properly paired %, and singletons %.”

Can you create a new dataframe called statsRatios that will only contain passed records for which the category value has a “%” sign? 🤔

ImportantCan you tell if this table of data is tidy? Is it in a long or wide format? 🤔

Let’s dive in the flagstat QC results

To approach this data ‘step-by-step’, we first just want to plot the mapping rate mapped %. For that, we will filter() the statsRatios table to keep only the records belonging “mapped %” category. Let’s call the resulting table mapRatios. 🤔

💭 Check the answer 🪂 
mapRatios <- statsRatios[statsRatios$category == "mapped %", ]
head(mapRatios)
##     passed failed category strainId
## 8    96.40     NA mapped %     1613
## 28   91.04     NA mapped %     1868
## 48   71.15     NA mapped %     4752
## 68   86.85     NA mapped %     5417
## 88   70.24     NA mapped %      685
## 108  38.18     NA mapped %      716

So now, we can plot the percentages (passed column) as y-values and the strain ids as x-values (aesthetics) and further add a geom_col() geom. Let’s plot it! 🤔

💭 Check the answer 🪂 
mapRatioP <- ggplot(data = mapRatios,
       mapping = aes(x = strainId, y = passed)) +
  geom_col(fill = "gold")
mapRatioP
## Warning: Removed 1 row containing missing values or values outside the scale range
## (`geom_col()`).
ImportantWhat do we learn from this regarding strains B218, 716, 685, …? 🤔

So this is not too bad but, the texts of the strain ids on the x-axis tend to overlap which is ugly. We could surely increase the overall width of the graph but this would take up space unnecessarily. Instaed, we can tweak the ggplot2 theme() parameters as such:

💭 Check the answer 🪂 
mapRatioP <- mapRatioP +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(hjust = 1, vjust = 1, angle = 45))
mapRatioP
## Warning: Removed 1 row containing missing values or values outside the scale range
## (`geom_col()`).

So we learnt already something regarding the mapping step but the statsRatios table contains far more info. Ideally, we would like to inspect everything to have a complete picture.

There are several ways to represent this. One is by adding a color aesthetic based on category and specifying a special position in geom_col()

💭 !! Check the answer !! 🪂 
statsRatiosP <-  ggplot(data=  statsRatios, mapping = aes(x = strainId, y = passed, fill = category)) +  geom_col(position = position_dodge()) +
  scale_fill_brewer(direction = 1) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(hjust = 1, vjust = 1, angle = 45),
        legend.position = "bottom")
statsRatiosP
## Warning: Removed 4 rows containing missing values or values outside the scale range
## (`geom_col()`).

Pivoting and exporting the flagstat data

For your non-bioinformaticians colleague to read the data, it would be far more convenient to “pivot” this dataframe from a ‘long’ format to a ‘wide’ one. We would like to have the values of the category column as separate columns (see the result below). For each strain (one row) the values from the passed column are pivoted to their cognate category. Furthermore, we sort the records in the table based on the strain id. The resulting statsRatiosWide table is displayed in html.

Can you try to figure out how to do that with tidyr::pivot_wider()? 🤔

💭 Check the answer 🪂 
statsRatiosWide <- tidyr::pivot_wider(
  statsRatios,
  id_cols=strainId,
  names_from = category,
  values_from = passed
)

statsRatiosWide <- statsRatiosWide[order(statsRatiosWide$strainId), ]

rmarkdown::paged_table(statsRatiosWide, options = list(cols.min.print = 4))

Finally, after so much troubles parsing the “flagstats” data, we would like to save the primary data flagstatsClean and the resulting statsRatiosWide tables as tsv files for subsequent scrutiny by other colleagues in the outDir. Can you do that with write.table ? 🤔

💭 Check the answer 🪂 
write.table(flagstatsClean, file = file.path(outDir, "algea_flagstats.tsv"), sep = "\t", quote = FALSE, col.names = TRUE, row.names = FALSE)

write.table(statsRatiosWide, file = file.path(outDir, "algea_flagstats_summary.tsv"), sep = "\t", quote = FALSE, col.names = TRUE, row.names = FALSE)

Examining the infered genetic diversity

Loading the vcf file data and extract a SNP matrix

# Take a look at the files
list.files(dataDir, recursive = TRUE)

vcfData <- read.vcfR(file.path(dataDir, "coding_data_CIBIG25/all_samples.vcf.gz"), verbose = FALSE)

glight <- vcfR2genlight(vcfData)
saveRDS(glight, file = file.path(outDir, "genotypes_genlight.rds"))

Run a PCA with genotypes data and plot the infered genetic diversity

The analysis workflow on this section is in large part inspired from the material provided by the Niklaus J. Grünwald lab in Population genetics and genomics in R

Just like with any topic in R and other programming languages, there are tons of other options to conduct this type of analysis. For example pegas is another R package dedicated to population genetic analysis.

if (!exists("glight")) glight <- readRDS(file.path(dataDir, "/coding_data_CIBIG25/genotypes_genlight.rds"))
nInd(glight)
## [1] 18
nLoc(glight)
## [1] 1375890
pca1 <- glPca(glight, nf = 20, parallel = TRUE, n.cores = 6)
print(pca1)
##  === PCA of genlight object ===
## Class: list of type glPca
## Call ($call):glPca(x = glight, nf = 20, parallel = TRUE, n.cores = 6)
## 
## Eigenvalues ($eig):
##  46781.29 19490.28 8333.119 7812.193 3221.12 2752.782 ...
## 
## Principal components ($scores):
##  matrix with 18 rows (individuals) and 18 columns (axes) 
## 
## Principal axes ($loadings):
##  matrix with 1375890 rows (SNPs) and 18 columns (axes)

scatter(pca1, posi="topright")

The reason we picked glPca() is because it is specialized for genotyping data. If you want to learn more about PCA in R, we advise you to examine specialized resources describing how to do statistical analysis with R using best practices. Here are a few resources as a starter:

  • The Handbook of Biological Statistics
  • datacamp

Revisiting the PCA results with ggplot2 plots

While the resulting plot is OK in preliminary stages. It is not entirely satisfactory because:

  • It is difficult to overlay strains metadata which would be useful to fully grasp the output.
  • stains labels are plotted on top of each others which hides part of the information.

Let’s try to come up with our own plots with ggplot2.

Metadata fixing and matching

First, it is time to include the strains metadata to this dataframe so that we can plot the samples along with their characteristics (sampling site, species …).

For that we need two objects: the metadata (algeaInfo) object and the PCA (pca1)object.

The Principal components matrix, thescores element from the pca1 object (list) are stored in pca1$scores

💭 Check the answer 🪂 
pcaScores <- as.data.frame(pca1$scores)

In this object the strain id are stored in the rownames, that are accessible using the rownames() function.

How would you create a strainId column with this information ?

💭 Check the answer 🪂 
rownames(pcaScores)
##  [1] "1613" "1868" "4752" "5417" "685"  "716"  "A1"   "A8"   "B1"   "B218"
## [11] "B8"   "C218" "C2"   "D119" "E2"   "E318" "G11"  "H44"
pcaScores$strainId <- rownames(pcaScores)

The strainId column contains the information about the algae strain but we need to extract it to match values in algeaInfo:

At this point, it may be a good idea to verify that strain IDs in both tables match, right? We could do that with set operations (?union). 🤔

💭 Check the answer 🪂 
pcaScores$strainId 
##  [1] "1613" "1868" "4752" "5417" "685"  "716"  "A1"   "A8"   "B1"   "B218"
## [11] "B8"   "C218" "C2"   "D119" "E2"   "E318" "G11"  "H44"
algeaInfo$`Strain ID`
##  [1] "A818"    "B218"    "B518"    "C218"    "E318"    "H718"    "D119"   
##  [8] "H44"     "A727"    "A827"    "RCC5417" "RCC1613" "RCC685"  "RCC1615"
## [15] "RCC1868" "RCC4222" "G11"     "C2"      "G2"      "E2"      "A8"     
## [22] "B8"      "A1"      "G8"      "C3"      "G5"      "RCC4752" "RCC716"

pcaScores$strainId %in% algeaInfo$`Strain ID`
##  [1] FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE  TRUE  TRUE FALSE  TRUE  TRUE  TRUE
## [13]  TRUE  TRUE  TRUE  TRUE  TRUE  TRUE

So it looks like the “RCC” prefix got striped out somehow in the read mapping data… We will fix that.

So first, we will modify the ids in this table (note that it is usually better to conduct reformatting of this kind of essential metadata table, right after loading into R in order to have a consistent object across the analysis). 🤔

TipYou can create a new strainId column filled with the result of substituting "RCC" in the strain ids Strain ID with "" using gsub()
💭 Check the answer 🪂 
algeaInfo$strainId <- gsub("RCC", "", algeaInfo$`Strain ID`)
algeaInfo$`Strain ID` <- NULL

can use dplyr join functions (type ?"mutate-joins" in the console). We will perform a left_join to bring strains info into the pcaScores tibble. The join will be done on the strainId key column that provides the ‘bridging’ information. 🤔

                       y = algeaInfo,
                       by = join_by("strainId" == "strainId")
                       )

ImportantAre all strains included in the genotyping described in the strains metadata table algeaInfo? 🤔

We should now have the required info in order to generate an informative plot. We start with a base ggplot2 plot assigned to the pp variable :

  • We represent the position of the strains in the PC space using the first and second PCs as points (geom_point()).
  • The shape aesthetic will be mapped to values in the Species column.
  • The color aesthetic will be mapped to values in the Sampling site column
  • Point size should be = 5 and transparency increased with alpha set to 0.3
💭 Check the answer 🪂 
pp <- ggplot(data = pcaScores,
             mapping =  aes(x = PC1,
                            y= PC2,
                            shape = Species,
                            color = `Sampling site`)
             ) +
  geom_point(size = 5, alpha = 0.3)
pp
## Warning: Removed 1 row containing missing values or values outside the scale range
## (`geom_point()`).

So now we are in a much better position to interpret the graph.

NoteThe strain belonging to the B. calidus species is isolated, consistent with an expected more distant relatedness with strains from the B. prasinos species. This is captured by PC2.
NoteStrains collected in the Baffin area tend to separate from the others. This is captured by PC1.

It would be nice to add strain ids in this plot. For that, let’s add some space around the data points in pp and modify the limits of the plot axis with xlim and ylim. Minimum x should be -250 and minmum y should be -150. We will also add an informative title. 🤔

💭 Check the answer 🪂 
pp <- pp +
  xlim(-250, NA) + ylim(-150, NA) +
  labs(title = "The algea genetic diversity is in part explained by sampling site")
pp
## Warning: Removed 1 row containing missing values or values outside the scale range
## (`geom_point()`).

To include strain ids as labels, we will add a text geom from the ggrepel package and tweak the parameters to force plotting of all overlapping labels.

pp <- pp +
  ggrepel::geom_text_repel(mapping = aes(label = strainId),
                           force = 20,
                           max.overlaps = 30)
pp
## Warning: Removed 1 row containing missing values or values outside the scale range
## (`geom_point()`).

This looks nice but lets use a more sober theme that is suitable for publications, like theme_light() 🤔

💭 Check the answer 🪂 
pp <- pp +
  theme_light()
pp
## Warning: Removed 1 row containing missing values or values outside the scale range
## (`geom_point()`).

We are perfectionists and clearly the values and ticks in the context of a PCA do not make much sense. We would like to avoid plotting them but we do not know how to tweak the plot to do that…

TipMay be we could ask an LLM like Chat GPT or Gemini. Can you figure out what prompts to use ?🤔
💭 Check the answer 🪂 
glue::glue("
*** Prompt1 ***
Hi,
Here is the code of a ggplot2 plot:
pp <- pp +
  ggrepel::geom_text_repel(mapping = aes(label = strainId),
                           force = 20,
                           max.overlaps = 30)
pp

*** Prompt2 ***
How can I avoid plotting the scales on the axis (numbers and tick marks)?
")

Let’s implement the solution suggested by the LLM:

💭 Check the answer 🪂 
pp <- pp +
    theme(axis.text =  element_blank(),
        axis.ticks = element_blank())
pp
## Warning: Removed 1 row containing missing values or values outside the scale range
## (`geom_point()`).

Make a composite plot as a final wrap up

Now let’s imagine we would like to make a composite plot of our best graphics to use as a Figure in a manuscript.

In R there are several packages that enables to do that. To name the main ones: - patchwork makes it ridiculously simple to combine separate ggplots into the same graphic. - cowplot helps with creating publication-quality figures, such as a set of themes, functions to align plots and arrange them into complex compound figures - aplot by the creator of amazing packages for phylogenetic trees plotting or complex heatmaps. This is our favorite because it works very well with these kind of atypical plots…

Let’s pick pp and statsRatiosP plots and plot them together in a plot named compoPlot. With the cowplot::plot_grid(), this is pretty easy… 🤔

💭 Check the answer 🪂 
compoPlot <- cowplot::plot_grid(statsRatiosP + ggtitle("An outlook on mapping QC"),
                                pp,
                                labels = c('A', 'B'), ncol = 1)
## Warning: Removed 4 rows containing missing values or values outside the scale range
## (`geom_col()`).
## Warning: Removed 1 row containing missing values or values outside the scale range
## (`geom_point()`).
compoPlot
Important

BTW, do you now have an hypothesis for the reason why only a limited fraction of the, say “716” strains reads, mapped to the reference? 🤔

OK, great but for the manuscript we would like to have a separate image file in the pdf format. Because compoPlot is a ggplot object. We can use a the dedicated ggplot2 function for this task.

💭 Check the answer 🪂 
ggsave(filename = file.path(outDir, "composite_plot.pdf"),
       plot = compoPlot,
       width = 6.5, height = 8, units = "in", dpi = 300)

Bonus: Distance tree of the samples

In biology, trees are a common way of representing the relationships between a diversity of samples.

Using the ape package, commonly used in phylogenetics and evolution, we will build a phenetic tree (distance-based from SNP data). Be careful, it’s not a model-based phylogeny !

💭 Check the answer 🪂 
# genetic distances (e.g., Euclidean on genlight)
Distances <- dist(glight)

# Neighbor-Joining tree
distance_tree <- nj(Distances)

# distance_tree is a "phylo" object
plot(distance_tree)
Important

The orientation of the resulting tree is arbitrary. How would you orient it now that we know a little bit more about the diversity of our samples ? 🤔

Using the ape package, commonly used in phylogenetics and evolution, we will build a phenetic tree (distance-based from SNP data). Be careful, it’s not a model-based phylogeny !

💭 Check the answer 🪂 
# Rooting the tree
rooted_tree <- root(distance_tree, "716")

# ploting the tree again
plot(rooted_tree)

In the same manner as for the PCA, it’s best to plot the phylogeny with some more information that we can get from the metadata table.1

💭 Check the answer 🪂 
# Where are the tip labels stored ?
str(rooted_tree)
## List of 4
##  $ edge       : int [1:33, 1:2] 19 28 27 26 25 21 20 20 21 22 ...
##  $ edge.length: num [1:33] 94.2 24.8 20.4 33.4 33 ...
##  $ tip.label  : chr [1:18] "1613" "1868" "4752" "5417" ...
##  $ Nnode      : int 16
##  - attr(*, "class")= chr "phylo"
##  - attr(*, "order")= chr "cladewise"

tips <- rooted_tree$tip.label

# what does the below return ?
match(rooted_tree$tip.label,algeaInfo$strainId)
##  [1] 12 15 27 11 13 28 23 21 NA  2 22  4 18  7 20  5 17  8

# the "species" column from the metadata table
algeaInfo$Species
##  [1] "B. prasinos"     "B. prasinos"     "B. prasinos"     "B. prasinos"    
##  [5] "B. prasinos"     "B. prasinos"     "B. prasinos"     "B. prasinos"    
##  [9] "B. prasinos"     "B. prasinos"     "B. prasinos"     "B. prasinos"    
## [13] "B. prasinos"     "B. prasinos"     "B. prasinos"     "B. prasinos"    
## [17] "B. prasinos"     "B. prasinos"     "B. prasinos"     "B. prasinos"    
## [21] "B. prasinos"     "B. prasinos"     "B. prasinos"     "Bathycoccus sp."
## [25] "Bathycoccus sp." "Bathycoccus sp." "B. prasinos"     "B. calidus"

# the species in the an order that matches the tree tips !
algeaInfo$Species[match(rooted_tree$tip.label,algeaInfo$strainId)]
##  [1] "B. prasinos" "B. prasinos" "B. prasinos" "B. prasinos" "B. prasinos"
##  [6] "B. calidus"  "B. prasinos" "B. prasinos" NA            "B. prasinos"
## [11] "B. prasinos" "B. prasinos" "B. prasinos" "B. prasinos" "B. prasinos"
## [16] "B. prasinos" "B. prasinos" "B. prasinos"

# we store it and do the same for the localization
tip_species <- algeaInfo$Species[match(rooted_tree$tip.label,algeaInfo$strainId)]
tip_localisation <- algeaInfo$`Sampling site`[match(rooted_tree$tip.label,algeaInfo$strainId)]

# we change the tip labels in the tree object
rooted_tree$tip.label <- paste0(tips,"_",tip_localisation)

# we now want two different symbols for the tips belonging to each species
# we start by producing a vector of one symbol
symbols <- rep(16,length(tip_species))
# and we modify those matching the second species
symbols[grepl("B. calidus", tip_species)] <- 17

symbols
##  [1] 16 16 16 16 16 17 16 16 16 16 16 16 16 16 16 16 16 16

# plot
print({
  
  plot(rooted_tree, cex = 0.9,show.tip.label = F)
  tiplabels(text = rooted_tree$tip.label, adj = 0, offset = 25, frame="none")
  tiplabels(pch = symbols, col = "black", bg = "white", cex = 1.2)
  
})
## NULL
